5061aaf3: Irreversible injury is marked by two things the cell cannot recover from: severe damage to the plasma membrane and to mitochondria (loss of ATP generation). Swelling, loss of microvilli, fatty change and ribosome detachment are all reversible changes.
8da338e1: Large, flocculent amorphous densities in mitochondria on electron microscopy are a sign of irreversible injury: the mitochondria can no longer recover and the cell is dying. Reversible injury shows only small densities and swelling.
49f61263: Hypoxic death of cells in solid organs produces coagulative necrosis: proteins are denatured, so the tissue keeps its architecture for days. The brain is the exception, where ischaemia produces liquefactive necrosis.
ec3a8258: Cerebral infarcts undergo liquefactive necrosis. Brain tissue has little supporting stroma and is rich in lipid, and enzymes from dead cells and microglia digest it into a fluid-filled cavity.
f92fb8e9: Fibrinoid necrosis is damage to blood vessel walls in which immune complexes and plasma proteins (including fibrin) deposit in the wall, giving a bright pink, smudgy appearance. It is typical of malignant hypertension and vasculitis. Tuberculosis gives caseous necrosis, brain infarcts liquefactive, pancreatitis fat necrosis.
06d3402c: Reversible injury shows cellular swelling, fatty change and membrane blebbing. Karyolysis (fading of the nucleus) is a nuclear change of necrosis, and large amorphous mitochondrial densities mean irreversible injury.
0edcd6ea: Hypoxia stops oxidative phosphorylation, so ATP falls; the ATP-dependent Na+/K+ pump fails, sodium and water enter, and the cell swells. Anaerobic glycolysis increases (not decreases) to make up for lost ATP, producing lactic acid, so intracellular pH falls rather than rises.
d56ca70d: Fatty change (steatosis) appears in organs that handle a lot of fat metabolism: mostly the liver, but also the heart, kidney and skeletal muscle. It is not a feature of brain or bone.
cd4ee4df: Alcohol, obesity, diabetes mellitus and protein malnutrition all cause fatty liver, either by increasing the fat delivered to the liver or by reducing the apoprotein needed to export it. Hyperthyroidism is not a cause.
7ce060b0: Necrosis is always pathological: the cell swells, its membranes rupture, its contents are digested by enzymes, and the leaked contents provoke inflammation. 'Always physiological' describes neither necrosis nor apoptosis.
47c4fbb7: All five are recognised causes of cell injury: oxygen deprivation, chemicals and drugs, infections, immune reactions, and genetic defects. Physical agents and nutritional imbalances complete the list.
c17015e5: BCL-2 is the main anti-apoptotic protein: it keeps the mitochondrial outer membrane intact so cytochrome c is not released. BAX and BAK are pro-apoptotic effectors, and BIM and PUMA are pro-apoptotic sensors.
0df7ac37: Removal of the tissue between the developing fingers and toes is a classic example of physiological apoptosis during embryogenesis. The other options are forms of pathological change.
02667270: Apoptosis is an energy-dependent (ATP-requiring) programme: the cell shrinks, the plasma membrane stays intact, and the cell breaks into apoptotic bodies that are eaten quickly. Because contents do not leak, there is no inflammation.
38b2565c: Apoptosis removes cells during embryogenesis, in hormone-dependent tissues when the hormone is withdrawn, in cells killed by cytotoxic T cells, and in self-reactive lymphocytes. Ischaemic death of solid tissue is coagulative necrosis, not apoptosis.
cd133c73: BCL-2, BCL-XL and MCL-1 are anti-apoptotic members of the BCL-2 family. BAX and BAK are pro-apoptotic: they form channels in the mitochondrial membrane that release cytochrome c.
eac1bbfd: Pathological apoptosis follows DNA damage, accumulation of misfolded proteins, some viral infections (Councilman bodies in viral hepatitis) and graft-versus-host disease. The core of a myocardial infarct dies by coagulative necrosis.
3e1a12c1: Reactive oxygen species come from ionising radiation, from phagocyte NADPH oxidase during the respiratory burst, from leakage in mitochondrial respiration, and from the Fenton reaction with free iron. Vitamin E is an antioxidant that removes them.
ba860385: Vitamins E and C, catalase and superoxide dismutase all neutralise free radicals. Free iron does the opposite: it generates hydroxyl radicals through the Fenton reaction.
16ab6c44: Free radicals peroxidise membrane lipids, oxidise and cross-link proteins, and damage DNA, all of which injure the cell. They make membranes less stable, not more.
d9058bed: The smooth muscle of the pregnant uterus enlarges by both mechanisms: oestrogen drives hyperplasia (more cells) and hypertrophy (bigger cells), because uterine smooth muscle can divide.
fac367d5: Chronic irritation from cigarette smoke turns the normal ciliated columnar epithelium of the bronchi into stratified squamous epithelium: squamous metaplasia. It is more resistant but loses mucus clearance, and can progress to cancer.
e8522484: Benign prostatic hyperplasia is driven by dihydrotestosterone, made from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase. This is why 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors shrink the prostate.
42f4bf5d: Physiological atrophy is a normal shrinking: the thymus after puberty, the notochord during development, and the uterus and ovary after menopause as hormones fall. Atrophy of denervated muscle is pathological.
6611cf63: Atrophy follows decreased workload, loss of nerve supply, reduced blood supply, poor nutrition, loss of hormonal stimulation, ageing and pressure. Increased hormonal stimulation causes the opposite: hyperplasia or hypertrophy.
6040964d: Metaplasia replaces one adult cell type with another more suited to the stress. It is reversible if the cause is removed, occurs in epithelium and in mesenchyme (for example bone forming in soft tissue), and can predispose to cancer, but it is not itself a neoplasm.
bc844a19: Hyperplasia is an increase in cell number. It is physiological in the breast at puberty, pathological when hormones or growth factors are in excess, and the basis of benign prostatic hyperplasia. It stays under control, so it is not a neoplasm, although it can be a soil for one.
0d6ee9e1: Dystrophic calcification is deposition of calcium in dead or damaged tissue while serum calcium stays normal. Hypercalcaemia, excess vitamin D, hyperparathyroidism and milk-alkali syndrome cause metastatic calcification instead.
8b470058: Metastatic calcification is deposition of calcium in normal tissues because serum calcium is high. Calcium deposits in atheroma, necrotic tissue and damaged valves are dystrophic.
076aa430: The Prussian blue (Perls) reaction turns iron in haemosiderin blue-black, so it is the stain used to show iron stores and iron overload.
7296e5c6: Amyloid stains pink-red with Congo red, and under polarised light it shows apple-green birefringence because of its regularly arranged fibrils. This is the diagnostic test.
d2dc644d: Dystrophic calcification happens in damaged or dead tissue: atheroma, damaged heart valves, caseous tuberculous lesions and fat necrosis. Hyperparathyroidism raises serum calcium and so causes metastatic calcification.
e3565852: Metastatic calcification favours tissues that lose acid and so have a relatively alkaline interior: the kidneys, lungs, gastric mucosa and systemic arteries. Calcium in atheroma is dystrophic.
d045f7aa: Haemosiderin is a golden-brown, iron-containing pigment from the breakdown of haemoglobin. It stains with Prussian blue and builds up in haemochromatosis and other iron overload. Bilirubin, not haemosiderin, is the bile pigment.
4c63e8ed: The first vascular change, lasting only seconds, is a brief arteriolar vasoconstriction (a neurogenic reflex). It is quickly followed by vasodilation, increased permeability, slowing of flow (stasis) and then margination and exudation.
74333799: Neutrophils dominate the first 6 to 24 hours because they are plentiful and respond fastest, but they are short-lived. By 24 to 48 hours they are replaced by monocytes, which mature into macrophages and survive longer.
d05d4212: The commonest cause of leakage is contraction of endothelial cells in postcapillary venules, opening gaps between them. It is triggered by histamine, bradykinin and leukotrienes, starts quickly and is short-lived (immediate transient response).
08699f82: IL-8 (CXCL8) is a chemokine that strongly attracts and activates neutrophils. Histamine, bradykinin and serotonin act mainly on vessels (dilation and permeability), and heparin is an anticoagulant.
6c5f880b: The cardinal signs are redness (rubor), heat (calor), swelling (tumor), pain (dolor) and loss of function (functio laesa). Itching is not one of them.
51ed57ee: Acute inflammation can resolve completely, heal by fibrosis, form an abscess (in pyogenic infection) or progress to chronic inflammation. It does not turn malignant; that needs genetic changes, although long-standing chronic inflammation can raise cancer risk.
bb1c69d6: Chronic inflammation is infiltrated by mononuclear cells (lymphocytes, macrophages and plasma cells) and shows tissue destruction with attempted repair, including angiogenesis and fibrosis. Neutrophil predominance is the hallmark of acute inflammation.
bf1868e7: Chronic inflammation lasts weeks to months, with mononuclear cells, tissue destruction and repair by fibrosis going on together. Exudate is typical of acute inflammation and is not always present in chronic inflammation.
6d6115dd: The membrane attack complex is assembled from C5b with C6, C7, C8 and multiple C9 molecules. It punches holes in the membranes of microbes (especially Neisseria). C3b is an opsonin, C1q starts the classical pathway, and C4b2a is the classical C3 convertase.
e539ce3a: Lipoxins are made from arachidonic acid by cells working together (for example neutrophils and platelets). They inhibit neutrophil recruitment and help switch off inflammation, so they are anti-inflammatory.
39388ca8: Fever is caused by the pyrogenic cytokines IL-1, TNF and IL-6. These raise prostaglandin E2 in the hypothalamus, which resets the temperature set point; this is why NSAIDs lower fever. Histamine is not a pyrogen.
881ebd12: Histamine, prostacyclin (PGI2), nitric oxide and PGE2 dilate vessels. LTC4 (with LTD4 and LTE4) causes vasoconstriction and bronchospasm while increasing permeability.
ef83c961: During the acute phase response the liver makes more CRP, fibrinogen, serum amyloid A and hepcidin, driven mainly by IL-6. Albumin is a negative acute phase protein: its level falls.
5cb39b3b: Leukotrienes are lipoxygenase products of arachidonic acid. LTB4 is a powerful neutrophil chemotactic agent; LTC4, LTD4 and LTE4 cause vasoconstriction, bronchospasm and increased permeability. Aspirin blocks cyclooxygenase, not lipoxygenase, so it does not stop leukotriene production.
2e6ce104: Oxygen-dependent killing depends on the phagocyte NADPH oxidase, which makes superoxide in the respiratory burst; myeloperoxidase then converts hydrogen peroxide to hypochlorite. Lysozyme, defensins, BPI and lactoferrin kill without oxygen.
36204a9d: Chronic granulomatous disease is an inherited defect of NADPH oxidase, so phagocytes cannot make reactive oxygen species. Patients get recurrent infections with catalase-positive organisms and form granulomas around the unkilled microbes.
4a80df3e: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type 1 is caused by a defective beta-2 integrin chain (CD18). Leukocytes cannot adhere firmly to endothelium or migrate into tissue, so there are recurrent bacterial infections with high blood neutrophil counts and delayed separation of the umbilical cord.
3384ab51: Chediak-Higashi syndrome is caused by mutation of the lysosomal trafficking regulator (LYST). Phagosomes fail to fuse with lysosomes, leukocytes contain giant granules, and patients have infections, albinism and nerve defects.
8c741224: Inflammatory IL-6 raises hepcidin, which blocks ferroportin. Iron is trapped in macrophages and gut cells and cannot reach the marrow, causing anaemia of chronic disease, with low serum iron but adequate or high ferritin.
b97b926e: The systemic (acute phase) response includes fever, leukocytosis, a raised ESR from more fibrinogen, and tachycardia. Hypoglycaemia is not a usual feature; stress hormones tend to raise blood glucose.
e25dbc8a: Neutrophilia follows bacterial infection, tissue necrosis such as infarction and burns, and corticosteroids (which release marginated neutrophils into the circulation). Typical viral infections cause lymphocytosis rather than neutrophilia.
aa63687c: Opsonins coat microbes so phagocytes can recognise and eat them: IgG, the complement fragment C3b, and collectins such as mannose-binding lectin. Albumin is not an opsonin.
feb62c2a: Oxygen-independent killing uses granule proteins: lysozyme, lactoferrin, defensins and bactericidal permeability-increasing protein (BPI). The myeloperoxidase-hydrogen peroxide system is oxygen-dependent.
c7a3e1c0: A granuloma is a pattern of type IV (cell-mediated, delayed) hypersensitivity: T cells release interferon-gamma, which activates macrophages that become epithelioid cells and giant cells.
de766c89: Sarcoidosis produces non-caseating granulomas, and its giant cells may contain asteroid bodies (star-shaped inclusions) and Schaumann bodies (laminated calcium). Tuberculosis and histoplasmosis typically caseate.
0d950065: The Kveim test (injection of sarcoid tissue extract, then biopsy for granulomas) was used to diagnose sarcoidosis. It is now obsolete; diagnosis rests on biopsy showing non-caseating granulomas with exclusion of other causes.
1b9b96c7: Tuberculosis, sarcoidosis, leprosy and Crohn disease all form granulomas. Ulcerative colitis does not: its inflammation is mucosal, with crypt abscesses but no granulomas, which helps tell it apart from Crohn disease.
b1eaa5a0: Caseating granulomas, with cheese-like necrotic centres, are typical of tuberculosis and some fungal infections such as histoplasmosis. Sarcoidosis, Crohn disease and foreign-body reactions form non-caseating granulomas.
bdf90363: Primary intention is healing of a clean wound with closely opposed edges, such as a sutured surgical incision: little granulation tissue and a thin scar. Large, gaping, infected or burned wounds heal by secondary intention.
daf6d6cc: Myofibroblasts are fibroblasts with smooth muscle features (actin filaments). They pull the wound edges together, which is why large wounds healing by secondary intention shrink markedly.
1ef7394e: Granulation tissue first lays down type III collagen, which is later remodelled and replaced by stronger type I collagen. This is why scar strength increases over weeks to months.
8a7eb6dc: A keloid is an overgrowth of collagen that extends beyond the original wound margin and does not regress. A hypertrophic scar stays within the margin, and exuberant granulation (proud flesh) is excess granulation tissue, not collagen.
f6f01725: All five delay healing: infection (the most important local factor), diabetes (poor blood supply and immunity), corticosteroids (suppress inflammation and collagen synthesis), foreign bodies, and vitamin C deficiency (needed to hydroxylate collagen).
2ccce02e: All five drive repair: EGF stimulates epithelial cells, PDGF attracts and stimulates fibroblasts and smooth muscle, VEGF drives new vessel growth, TGF-beta promotes collagen deposition and fibrosis, and FGF supports angiogenesis and fibroblast growth.
60a09607: Secondary intention follows large tissue loss: there is much more granulation tissue and more wound contraction, so it leaves a larger scar, not a smaller one.
7a6119d3: All five are complications of healing: wound dehiscence (rupture), keloid (excess collagen), contracture (deforming contraction, for example after burns), incisional hernia, and Marjolin ulcer (squamous cell carcinoma arising in a chronic scar or ulcer).
fe44dad3: In heart failure, raised venous pressure increases capillary hydrostatic pressure, and reduced renal blood flow activates renin-angiotensin-aldosterone, so the kidneys retain sodium and water. Both push fluid into the tissues.
66f81749: Filarial worms block lymphatics. Protein-rich lymph collects and the tissue becomes fibrotic, so the swelling does not pit on pressure; in advanced cases it is called elephantiasis.
de1664cf: Anasarca is severe, generalised oedema of the subcutaneous tissues throughout the body, often with fluid in the body cavities, as seen in nephrotic syndrome or severe heart failure.
61853e60: In nephrotic syndrome, heavy proteinuria lowers serum albumin, so plasma oncotic pressure falls and fluid moves into the tissues. Secondary sodium retention adds to it.
ea44f744: Heart failure, nephrotic syndrome, cirrhosis and hypoalbuminaemia all cause pitting oedema: protein-poor fluid that can be pushed aside. Chronic lymphatic obstruction gives protein-rich, fibrotic, non-pitting oedema.
c566fc8f: A transudate is a protein-poor ultrafiltrate from altered pressure, with low specific gravity (below 1.012) and few cells. It is not inflammatory and does not clot, because it lacks fibrinogen.
f66c9415: An exudate comes from inflammation-induced leaky vessels: it is rich in protein, has a specific gravity above 1.020 and contains many cells. It is often cloudy (purulent if many neutrophils), not always clear.
336ef795: Lines of Zahn are alternating pale layers (platelets and fibrin) and dark layers (red cells) formed as a thrombus grows in flowing blood. They show it formed during life, unlike a postmortem clot.
929372eb: Factor V Leiden, a point mutation that makes factor V resistant to inactivation by activated protein C, is the commonest inherited cause of thrombophilia in people of European descent.
11622edd: Nonbacterial thrombotic (marantic) endocarditis is small, sterile vegetations on normal valves in a hypercoagulable state, most often with cancer (especially mucinous adenocarcinoma) or debilitating illness.
e6fb0311: Libman-Sacks endocarditis is small, sterile vegetations on either side of the valve leaflets in systemic lupus erythematosus.
3e4e9ea9: Arterial thrombi start at sites of endothelial injury, most often over atheroma, in fast-flowing blood. They are pale (mostly platelets and fibrin), often mural in the heart and aorta, and show lines of Zahn. They are not mostly red; that describes venous thrombi.
a31a06e9: Venous thrombi form where blood is slow (stasis), usually in leg veins. They contain many red cells trapped in fibrin, so they are red, and they usually occlude the vein. White describes arterial thrombi.
a415b5ec: A thrombus can grow (propagate), break off as an embolus, be dissolved by fibrinolysis, or be organised by ingrowth of granulation tissue, sometimes recanalising. An old organised thrombus can also calcify, forming a phlebolith in veins.
13225115: A postmortem clot is gelatinous, with a dark red lower part (currant jelly) and a yellow upper part (chicken fat) from red cells settling. It is smooth and shiny, not attached to the vessel wall and easily removed. Lines of Zahn belong to antemortem thrombi.
5a5e0a9e: Factors II, VII, IX and X (with proteins C and S) need vitamin K for gamma-carboxylation, which is why warfarin lowers them. Factor VIII is not vitamin K-dependent.
3db699bc: A thrombus is a mass made from blood constituents: platelets, fibrin, red cells and leukocytes. Fat is not a component; fat in a vessel is a fat embolus.
59bd1dea: Almost all emboli are dislodged thrombi (thromboemboli), most often from deep leg veins to the lungs. Fat, air, amniotic fluid and tumour emboli are much less common.
7cd49dc5: A saddle embolus is a large thromboembolus that straddles the bifurcation of the main pulmonary artery, and it can cause sudden death.
b50c09a4: Fat embolism syndrome follows long-bone fractures: within one to three days there is breathlessness (pulmonary insufficiency), neurological signs such as confusion, and a petechial rash, with anaemia and thrombocytopenia.
30ece71d: White (pale, anaemic) infarcts occur in solid organs with end-arterial supply, such as the heart, spleen and kidney, where solid tissue limits bleeding into the dead area. The lung, intestine and twisted ovary give red infarcts.
fdacc280: Red (haemorrhagic) infarcts occur with venous occlusion (such as ovarian torsion), in loose tissue like lung, in organs with a dual circulation (lung, intestine), and where flow returns to dead tissue (reperfusion). The heart gives white infarcts.
93fd0fbe: Fat embolism follows long-bone fractures (rich in fatty marrow), and less often extensive soft tissue trauma, burns and liposuction. Hypertension does not cause it.
0ca73966: More than about 100 mL of air is usually needed to cause harm in the circulation. Air can enter through neck vein injury, obstetric procedures or laparoscopy. Decompression sickness (caisson disease in divers) is gas coming out of solution when pressure falls quickly.
47cc9398: Shock passes through three stages: a non-progressive (compensated) stage, where reflexes keep the organs perfused; a progressive stage with tissue hypoperfusion and acidosis; and an irreversible stage with severe cell injury.
b38a5a2e: 'Shock lung' is diffuse alveolar damage producing acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), a common complication of shock, especially septic shock.
c3de1a65: Septic shock comes from microbial products and cytokines: widespread vasodilation, endothelial injury and activation, and a tendency to DIC. Early on the skin is warm and flushed. Jugular venous pressure is low, not raised, because circulating volume is relatively low.
98cc6238: Irreversible shock has widespread cellular damage, lactic acidosis, acute tubular necrosis and hypotension that no longer responds to treatment. Rapid recovery does not happen at this stage, even if blood pressure is restored.
98d51848: Neurogenic shock follows spinal cord injury or anaesthetic accidents. Loss of sympathetic tone causes vasodilation and pooling of blood, often with bradycardia. Total blood volume is normal, so it is not hypovolaemic shock.
26da1f1d: Marfan syndrome is caused by mutations in FBN1, the gene for fibrillin-1, a scaffold for elastic fibres. Loss of fibrillin also increases TGF-beta activity. The result is tall stature, lens dislocation and aortic dilatation and dissection.
0a377c80: Huntington disease is autosomal dominant: one mutant copy (an expanded CAG repeat in huntingtin) is enough. Cystic fibrosis, thalassaemia, sickle cell anaemia and phenylketonuria are autosomal recessive.
174f7c28: Cystic fibrosis is autosomal recessive, so both CFTR copies must be mutated. Neurofibromatosis, Marfan syndrome, adult polycystic kidney disease and Huntington disease are autosomal dominant.
3eaca641: Haemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency) is X-linked recessive: it mostly affects males, and carrier females are usually unaffected.
4b633700: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is caused by loss of dystrophin, which links the muscle cytoskeleton to the cell membrane. Without it, muscle fibres are damaged during contraction.
e7620122: The commonest CFTR mutation is deletion of three nucleotides that removes phenylalanine at position 508 (delta F508). The protein misfolds and is destroyed before reaching the cell surface.
94200b66: Fragile X syndrome is caused by expansion of a CGG trinucleotide repeat in FMR1, which silences the gene. It is a leading inherited cause of intellectual disability in males.
73baa598: Fabry disease (alpha-galactosidase A deficiency) is the X-linked lysosomal storage disease. Gaucher, Tay-Sachs, Niemann-Pick and Pompe diseases are autosomal recessive.
b3b53ebe: Marfan syndrome, neurofibromatosis, Huntington disease and adult polycystic kidney disease are autosomal dominant. Sickle cell anaemia is autosomal recessive.
d8bb8e29: Phenylketonuria, cystic fibrosis, thalassaemia and sickle cell anaemia are autosomal recessive (enzyme or haemoglobin defects are typically recessive). Hunter syndrome (MPS II) is X-linked recessive.
2af28009: Haemophilia B, G6PD deficiency, Lesch-Nyhan syndrome and Duchenne muscular dystrophy are X-linked recessive. Wilson disease is autosomal recessive.
65be76dd: Mitochondrial DNA comes only from the egg, so these disorders pass from the mother to all her children of either sex, never from the father. Cells carry a mix of normal and mutant mitochondria (heteroplasmy). Leber hereditary optic neuropathy is the classic example.
e13ac984: About 95% of Down syndrome is trisomy 21 from meiotic nondisjunction, mostly in the egg and rising with maternal age. Robertsonian translocation and mosaicism account for the rest.
51add2b2: Klinefelter syndrome is most often 47,XXY: a male with an extra X chromosome, causing hypogonadism.
0658bb98: Turner syndrome is most often 45,X (complete loss of one X chromosome), causing short stature and ovarian failure. Mosaicism and structural X abnormalities make up the rest.
8eb343d0: The Philadelphia chromosome is the shortened chromosome 22 from the t(9;22) translocation, which creates the BCR-ABL fusion gene, a constantly active tyrosine kinase. It is the hallmark of chronic myeloid leukaemia.
f82e558f: Cri-du-chat syndrome is caused by deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p-). Affected infants have a high-pitched, cat-like cry, microcephaly and intellectual disability.
b9f07f13: DiGeorge syndrome is caused by a deletion at 22q11.2. It leads to thymic hypoplasia (T-cell deficiency), absent parathyroids (hypocalcaemia) and conotruncal heart defects.
2b8b34a0: All five apply to Down syndrome: trisomy 21, a single palmar crease, endocardial cushion (AV canal) defects, a higher risk of acute leukaemia, and early Alzheimer disease (the amyloid precursor protein gene is on chromosome 21).
230391d7: Turner syndrome causes short stature, a webbed neck, streak ovaries and coarctation of the aorta. With only one X chromosome there is nothing to inactivate, so no Barr body forms.
467a2165: Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) causes small testes with hypogonadism, gynaecomastia and tall stature with long legs. The extra X is inactivated, so a Barr body is present. The phenotype is male.
b528bd81: Edwards syndrome is trisomy 18 and Patau syndrome is trisomy 13. Both are severe, and most affected infants die in the first year, so survival to adulthood is not expected. Rocker-bottom feet are typical of Edwards syndrome.
